job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Esther Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a room in Bristol with my friend Tamsin, in a house with two other people, and my day starts with coffee and a to-do list on my phone. I spend the mornings on applications and on a little side project, a bot that reads local event pages and posts a daily digest, which has about forty subscribers. In the afternoon I do small freelance jobs, like fixing someone's website or cleaning a spreadsheet, for twenty or thirty pounds each, and in the evening I read about whatever new AI tool came out that week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was your final project?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Computer science, passed with an average result. My final project was a bus timetable app for the city, which real people used for about a month before the council changed its data format and broke it. I had no internship because I applied to forty places in second year and got no reply, and I worked in a bar instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that suits me fine, and I'd probably be a little disappointed, because I've bet a lot of my time on this stuff. At work or in interviews I'd say AI is a useful tool, nothing magic. Online I'd post a how-to on automating the boring bits of a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means the job market stays as tight as it is, and my AI skills don't give me an edge. If AI is mostly hype, then everyone competes for the same few junior roles, and I'm one more pass degree with no internship. My side income still helps, but it won't cover rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the freelance jobs going and aim at ten new clients, mostly small shops and clubs. I'd apply for fifteen jobs a week, including ones outside software, like data entry and support roles that lead somewhere. I'd also finally finish the digest bot and try charging a few pounds a month for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. I'm not scared of this one, but I'm not hopeful either. I'd feel I'm treading water with a large loan on my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be a little disappointed. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the part of me that likes building things loves that the tools are getting good. If it all fizzled, I'd feel I'd spent three years being a bit too early. And I'd have nothing to show that makes me different from everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do the freelance jobs bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month it was about two hundred and eighty pounds, on a good week sixty. Rent for my share is three hundred and ten, so I'd be short without the bar shifts I still pick up twice a week. It's real money but it's not a living.

Online I'd post a how-to on automating boring jobs for small businesses.
think: If AI is mostly hype, my **AI skills** give no edge.
I'm one more pass degree with no internship, and side income won't cover rent.

Apply for fifteen jobs a week, including data and support roles.
Finish my digest bot and try charging **a few pounds** a month.

Finish the event digest bot and start charging subscribers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and people should get their hands on the tools early. At interviews I'd show my bots and say I can do the work of a small team with one person and a good setup. Online I'd write about how to stay useful as a person who checks and directs the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this one cuts both ways for me. My own kind of job, junior coding and testing, is exactly what gets squeezed. But I'm also the person who can show a firm how to use the new tools, so I might find a gap as an AI helper in a small company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch small local firms: invoices, customer emails and booking systems set up with AI, for a monthly fee. I'd build two or three demo projects and put them online. If I don't land clients in six months, I'd apply to support roles at software firms and move up from there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy together. I think I'm better placed than most people my age, but I know a hundred other graduates are pitching the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge the small firms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start at a hundred and fifty a month for a package, like an inbox helper and a booking form. Cheaper than hiring, but enough to cover my rent if I land three clients. I know I'd have to be reliable, because one broken thing and they'd cancel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most about that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Trust, honestly. A shop owner has no reason to believe a twenty-three-year-old with a pass degree. I'd need a couple of references from the freelance jobs and maybe a local business group to vouch for me.

fieldNote: She turns disruption into a business plan, a very **adaptive** reflex.

steps.text: Pitch local shops a monthly AI package for invoices and bookings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and nobody's ready, so we need rules and support now. Online I'd explain it in plain words because most people have no idea. To my family I'd say, don't panic, but make sure we've got savings and a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means the thinking jobs I trained for are gone before I get my first one. A firm could run the digest bot, the websites and the spreadsheets at no cost, so my freelance work goes too. I'd have maybe a year of any income before the clients just ask the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending to the bone, which means no more takeaway and no bar nights. I'd chase every freelance job I can in the next twelve months, and put all of it into a savings pot. And I'd look at hands-on routes that last longer, like installing smart home gear or working in a lab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really frightened. The thing I'm good at is the thing that disappears first. I'd feel I'd ridden a wave up and it was about to break over me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call my mum in Swindon and say it straight: I might not find a graduate job, and I might have to come home. She'd say of course I can, but there's no spare money there, and she'd worry. I'd tell her I'm making a plan, even if I'm not sure it's a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two-year warning change about how you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It stops me gambling. Right now I'd try a risky product and see. With two years I'd put everything into cash and cheap, practical skills, because I can't afford a failure. It's the first time I'd choose safe over clever.

fieldNote: The **two-year** deadline pulls her from risk-taking to saving.

Home with her mother is the fallback, but there is no spare money.

Take every small freelance job for twelve months
Apply for smart home installer and lab technician jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to be dangerous and short enough to plan. I'd tell people to learn the tools, build a cushion and talk to their local representatives. Online I'd post a plain list of what people can do each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years lets me turn my skills into something solid. I could land a first job in the next year, then use the tools to move quickly through it. By 2031 I'd have a few years of experience and savings, which beats where I am now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any first job that lets me practise, even a support role, and move around inside it. I'd keep a small freelance practice for the extra income. And I'd save five hundred a quarter, even if I have to skip the bar nights and sell my old laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, cautiously good. I'd feel active rather than just afraid. Five years gives a story where I'm not the victim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year, month by month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first three months I'd just get a job. Months four to eight, I'd learn how the company works and which tasks AI already handles. The last four, I'd move into something that checks or directs the machine, since that's where junior people would still be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do when AGI actually arrives in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably something hands-on or people-facing, like running training for other staff, or a role that needs a human signature. I'd also keep my savings in a boring account. By then I'd want a year's rent in the bank.

I'd post a plain list of what people can do each year.

With a job and savings by 2031, I'd be far ahead of where I am.

steps.text: Take any first job that lets me practise and move around

Keep a small freelance practice on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it well, if we start now. I'd say there should be national plans, and that students deserve to hear straight about what's coming. Online I'd probably tell my own story, because I think it helps people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years is almost the best case for someone like me. I could have a first job, a second job and maybe start a small company before AGI. I'd be thirty-three in 2036, with a career and savings, and the debt cleared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job in the next year and then aim for a role that mixes people and tech, like customer solutions. I'd make one new thing a year, a small product or a course, to build a name. I'd also pay the loan down by two thousand a year and put a bit into shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a hum of excitement. This is the one where I get to be curious without being scared. I'd still know it could go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change what you'd study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd do a part-time master's in something like human-computer interaction or data ethics. Those need a human who understands people, which holds up better. If someone else paid for half I'd do it sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the danger you'd watch for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. If everything's fine for six or seven years, I'd forget about 2036 and be caught flat-footed. So I'd put a date in my diary every January and ask: what have I done this year that a machine can't?

I'd tell students straight what's coming and share my own story online.
think: Ten years is almost the **best case** for someone like me.
I could have two jobs, a small company and the debt cleared by thirty-three.

fieldNote: Her only **calm** answer; she expects to have work, savings and a cleared loan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My skills are exactly what that world replaces first, and I'd have no time to rebuild. What would help is cheap retraining paid by the companies that gain, and employers willing to take a chance on a junior who can prove they're useful.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being good with AI isn't a safe place to stand, which is what people assume. I'm using the tools every day, and I still don't have a job. Being prepared and being employed are not the same thing. I'd like people to know that.

headlineQuote: I'm using the tools every day, and I still don't have a job. Being prepared and being employed are not the same thing.
portrait: **Esther**, 23, passed computer science without an internship and shares a room in Bristol with her friend Tamsin.
She earns about **280 pounds** a month freelancing and runs a small digest bot with forty subscribers.
Progressive and curious, she uses AI tools every day and picks up new ones **early**.
Her plans are practical: pitch small firms, build demos, then switch to saving and cheap skills if the warning is short.
Her mood runs from anxious to alarmed in the two-year world and calm only in the ten-year one.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world worries her most, because her skills are what gets replaced first.
She'd have no time to rebuild and no cushion to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, **paid retraining** funded by the firms that gain from AI.
Employers willing to take a chance on a junior who can prove they're useful.
